analysis.one_liner: Requires airlines to feed, inform, and compensate delayed passengers and forces big carriers to give up landing slots to new competitors.
analysis.headline: The bill never got a vote in the House; it was referred to the Aviation Subcommittee, held two hearings in March 1999, and died there when the Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have required airlines to give passengers food, water, restrooms, and medical access when they are stuck on a plane, and to pay each traveler double the fare for delays of two to three hours and more after that. It would have raised the floor on what airlines owe for lost or damaged luggage, guaranteed alternate travel or refunds to passengers bumped from oversold flights, and given the Transportation Department power to redistribute landing slots at the busiest airports to new, smaller airlines. It also required public reports ranking the most and least expensive routes and the most concentrated airports.
analysis.who_benefits: Airline passengers gain enforceable rights: care while stuck on the tarmac, notice of delays, compensation worth twice their fare for excessive delays, at least $2,500 in liability for lost or damaged bags, and refunds or alternate travel when bumped. Travelers in markets dominated by one carrier would gain from slot auctions opening the busiest airports to new, lower-fare airlines, and the public would get quarterly data on which routes and airports are the most expensive and concentrated.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Airline passengers and travelers in monopoly markets

how_it_helps.text: Requires carriers to ensure passengers have food, water, restroom access, and emergency medical services on boarded flights, with carrier authority suspended for failure to file an emergency plan [S2, S3].

Makes airlines liable to every passenger for excessive delays: 200% of the fare for delays over two but under three hours, plus an additional 100% of the fare per hour beyond three hours, with exceptions for air-traffic-control directives and safety/mechanical problems [S2, S3].

Bars airlines from limiting liability for lost, damaged, or delayed luggage to less than $2,500 per passenger, and requires alternate transportation plus a refund or voucher for passengers involuntarily bumped from oversold flights when the alternate arrival is more than two hours late [S2, S3].

Directs the Transportation Secretary to withdraw up to 10% of major carriers' grandfathered slots at slot-controlled airports for auction, open only to new-entrant and limited incumbent carriers, with proceeds going to the Airport and Airway Trust Fund; the bill's findings note new entrants held fewer than 45 of more than 3,100 slots at the four high-density airports and that concentrated markets charge fares more than 20% higher [S3].

Requires quarterly public reports ranking the ten most and least expensive domestic routes and ranking large hub airports by market concentration, plus a study of whether small carriers can get gates on equal terms [S2, S3].

analysis.who_pays: Major incumbent airlines pay: they would owe cash compensation for long delays, higher minimum liability for lost bags, civil penalties up to $10,000 for unfair competitive practices, and would periodically lose grandfathered landing slots at the four slot-controlled airports to auction for new entrants. Some of these costs would likely flow into ticket prices, and the bill's own drafters acknowledged weather-related delays can be outside a carrier's control.
analysis.who_pays_short: Major incumbent airlines and their shareholders

drawbacks.text: Delay compensation is strict liability: an airline would owe every passenger double the fare for a two-hour-plus delay even when the cause was weather or congestion beyond its control, since the exceptions apply only to air-traffic-control directives and mechanical/safety problems [S3].

Forcing food, water, and restroom access on aircraft that frequently cannot depart raises real operational and safety questions, and carriers could pass compliance and compensation costs on through fares [S3].

Auctioning off incumbent carriers' slots up to 5% at a time could add turbulence to schedules at already congested airports, and only new-entrant and limited incumbent carriers may bid, restricting the auction market by design [S2, S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The passenger protections are concrete and enforceable but not free: strict delay liability and on-board care requirements are blunt instruments, and honest supporters would concede weather delays and congestion are often not the airline's fault. The slot-auction title is the more structural change, aimed at documented concentration (the bill cites GAO findings of fares more than 20% higher in concentrated markets), but its benefit to travelers would depend on whether new entrants can actually use the slots profitably. On balance the bill trades real passenger rights and a shot at more competition for costs and scheduling risk borne by the major carriers and, partly, by fares.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the House Transportation and Infrastructure Committee and its Aviation Subcommittee, held two hearings in March 1999, and never advanced to a markup or floor vote before the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. John Dingell introduced the bill on February 23, 1999, and it was referred to the House Committee on Transportation and Infrastructure the same day [S1, S5].
The next day it was referred to the Subcommittee on Aviation, which held hearings on March 10 and March 17, 1999 [S5].
No further action was taken: the bill never received a subcommittee vote, a full committee markup, or a floor vote, and it died when the 106th Congress ended [S1, S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Major incumbent airlines are better off: they kept their grandfathered slots at the four slot-controlled airports free of auction exposure and never faced statutory delay compensation, the $2,500 baggage-liability floor, or mandatory on-board care requirements. Passengers remained on a complaint-and-voluntary-commitment system instead.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Major incumbent airlines kept their slots

for.name: Rep. John D. Dingell
for.role: Sponsor, House Ranking Member (Energy and Commerce)
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and made introductory remarks on the House floor.

for.name: 9 House cosponsors (8 Democrats, 1 Republican)
for.what_they_did: Signed on as cosponsors, giving the bill bipartisan sponsorship.

against.name: House Transportation and Infrastructure Committee / Aviation Subcommittee
against.what_they_did: Referred the bill to the Aviation Subcommittee and took no action beyond two hearings; no markup, no vote, no report was ever scheduled.

against.name: Major U.S. airlines
against.what_they_did: Opposed legislated passenger rights in this period and pushed a voluntary customer-service program as an alternative; the industry faced the bill's delay liability, slot auctions, and unfair-competition penalties directly.

sides.party_line_note: The bill never reached a vote, so there is no roll-call record; its 9 cosponsors were 8 Democrats and 1 Republican, and the committee that let it stall was controlled by Republicans.

industries.note: The bill imposes cash liability for long delays, a $2,500 minimum baggage-liability floor, up to $10,000 penalties for unfair competitive practices, and periodic withdrawal of grandfathered slots at high-density airports for auction to new entrants. Its interests in this bill run against passenger rights and against opening hub markets to competition.

New entrants held fewer than 45 of more than 3,100 slots at the four slot-controlled airports; the bill reserves auctioned slots exclusively for them, giving low-fare carriers a way into hub markets. Their gain comes through more competition and lower fares, which also benefits travelers.

industries.industry: Airports and the aviation system (Airport and Airway Trust Fund)
industries.note: Auction proceeds and escrow interest flow into the Airport and Airway Trust Fund, recovering for the public a portion of slot value given to carriers free in 1985. Auction administration would impose some cost and scheduling disruption at congested airports.
